did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a heading attributing it to Asaph and mentioning the phrase “upon the Gittith”; the exact meaning of this phrase is not explained in the psalm itself.
The opening invites Israel to shout for joy to the God of Jacob and rejoice in him, emphasizing that praise is expressed loudly and with communal joy.
Several musical instruments are mentioned in the verse: the tambourine, lyre, and harp. Praise is thus portrayed as an act combining singing, instrumental music, and rhythm.

The psalm commands the blowing of the shofar “at the New Moon” and “at the full moon,” on a festival day. These words connect the shofar blast with a festive time in the calendar, although the verse does not specify exactly which festival it is.

The festival and the sounding of the shofar are presented as “a statute for Israel” and “an ordinance of the God of Jacob”—that is, as part of a binding obligation or established order for the nation.

The verse mentions Joseph and his departure from the land of Egypt, and adds the phrase “I heard a language I did not understand.” The text suggests a connection between Joseph, Egypt, and a language unfamiliar to the speaker.
The images of removing the burden from the shoulder and freeing the hands from the basket describe Israel’s release from hard labor and slavery.

The LORD describes rescuing Israel in a time of trouble and answering from “the hiding place of thunder.” He then recalls the testing at the waters of Meribah—an event in which water was connected with trial and testing.

The appeal “Hear, my people” repeats the demand that Israel listen to God’s testimony. Immediately afterward comes the prohibition against having a foreign god in Israel or bowing down to an alien deity.
The LORD recalls that he brought Israel out of Egypt and then offers: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it”—an image of his promise to provide for the people if they turn to him.
The psalm presents Israel’s disobedience: the people did not listen to the LORD’s voice and would not obey him. Therefore, the LORD describes Israel as following its own stubborn heart and counsel.

The final verses present a conditional outcome: if Israel had listened to the LORD, he would have quickly subdued its enemies, and Israel would have enjoyed an abundance of wheat and honey flowing from the rock.
